article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Netflix has preemptively acquired Canopy , a horror-thriller creature feature spec from Brandon Feldman , sources tell Deadline.

Reps for Netflix declined comment. We’re told this was a six-figure deal; Verve held the auction.

Comped to films like Apex , Predator and The Shallows , Canopy follows a botanist searching for a rare medical cure in the uncharted Amazon canopy who must survive a terrifying, undiscovered apex predator after she is offered as a sacrifice by a local village.

Related Stories

Top 50 Classic Horror Movies

Top 50 Halloween Movies Photo Gallery: Creepy Classics From ‘Psycho,’ ‘The Shining’ To ‘Obsession’ & ‘Get Out’

Juror #2 ‘s Adam Goodman and Matt Skiena will produce via Dichotomy. They snapped up the script after it began generating buzz when posted to The Black List website.

Watch on Deadline

Feldman’s romantic-comedy Marriage Material — co-written with Ben Agron, and starring Emma Roberts and Matt Rife — is set up with BuzzFeed Studios and Capstone Pictures. The duo were also hired to write a rom-com for Storyboard Entertainment.

Feldman has optioned other scripts to Rebel Way Entertainment, Minds Eye Entertainment, and Belga Studios. He’s represented by Verve, John Dunne at Independent Artists Media, and Mitchel Ostrove at Yorn, Levine, Barnes.

editorial_title_zh: ARTnews 庆祝 2026 年度“全球前 200 名收藏家”特刊发布
editorial_excerpt_zh: 前 200 名收藏家埃斯特雷利塔·布罗德斯基（Estrellita Brodsky）与贝基·戈赫曼（Becky Gochman）共同主持了此次活动。
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "9月29日，ARTnews在纽约范德堡一号大厦（Summit New York 1 Vanderbilt）庆祝了其第37期年度“全球前200名收藏家”榜单的发布，活动现场展示了从克莱斯勒大厦、摩根大通大厦到帝国大厦令人印象深刻的纽约天际线景观。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当晚的共同主持者包括：赫什霍恩博物馆和雕塑园（Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden）主席、切尔西“另一个空间”（Another Space）联合创始人埃斯特雷利塔·布罗德斯基，以及戈赫曼家族收藏（Gochman Family Collection）联合创始人贝基·戈赫曼——该收藏将于下个月在纽约卡托纳开设名为 Branchline 的展览空间。", "links": [{"text": "Branchline", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/gochman-family-collection-branchline-opening-date-1234801692/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在致辞中，戈赫曼谈到了艺术家在艺术世界中扮演的核心角色。“我想今晚在这里发表一个声明，没有艺术家，我们就不会站在这里，”她说道，“在我们心中，艺术家是最重要的，尊重艺术家是我们能做最好的事情之一。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "布罗德斯基强调了收藏家在支持艺术家方面所起的作用。“我收藏了几十年，并试图通过我的慈善事业，在全球语境下促进人们对拉丁美洲及其侨民艺术家的理解，这样我们就不会被排除在讨论之外，”她说道，“我们使命中非常重要的一部分就是借出这些作品。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "此次发布派对与 The Balvenie、Reckoner Art Finance 和 Cygnet 合作呈现。整个晚上，来宾们受邀品尝了一系列鸡尾酒以及 The Balvenie 的四种不同威士忌，该品牌最近曾与艺术家丹尼尔·阿尔诗（Daniel Arsham）合作，为 The 1931 Collection 打造了特别酒盒。Reckoner Art Finance 首席执行官劳拉·达梅姆（Laura Damême）出席了活动，向收藏家们讲解了他们如何利用已有的艺术品通过艺术品抵押贷款来扩大收藏。作为一个诞生于艺术与音乐世界的烈酒品牌，Cygnet 提供了定制鸡尾酒，其中包括 The Collector’s Royale 22。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "点击上方幻灯片即可查看当晚的照片。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
On September 29, ARTnews celebrated the launch of the 37th edition of our annual Top 200 Collectors list at Summit New York 1 Vanderbilt, which featured impressive views of the New York skyline from the Chrysler Building to the JPMorgan Chase Tower to the Empire State Building.

The evening’s cohosts were Estrellita Brodsky, chair of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden and cofounder of Another Space in Chelsea, and Becky Gochman, cofounder of the Gochman Family Collection, which will open Branchline , an exhibition space in Katonah, New York, next month.

During remarks, Gochman spoke about the central role artists play in the art world. “I would like to make a statement here tonight that we wouldn’t be here without the artists,” she said. “The artists, in our minds, are the most important, and to defer to the artists is one of the best things that we can do.”

Brodsky highlighted the role that collectors play in supporting artists. “I’ve been collecting for decades and trying, through my philanthropy, to promote an understanding of the artists from Latin America and its diaspora within a global context so that we’re not left out of discussion,” she said. “A very important part of our mission is to lend the works out.”

The launch party was presented in collaboration with The Balvenie, Reckoner Art Finance, and Cygnet. Throughout the evening, guests were invited to enjoy a series of cocktails and four different expressions of The Balvenie, which recently collaborated with artist Daniel Arsham on a special case for The 1931 Collection. Reckoner Art Finance CEO Laura Damême was on hand to speak to collectors about how they can use the art they already own to grow their collections through art-backed lending. A spirit born from the worlds of art and music, Cygnet offered bespoke cocktails, including The Collector’s Royale 22.

Click the slideshow above to see photos from the evening.

Disponible à compter de ce samedi 7 novembre, Fisheye #79 retrace le parcours des photographes à travers son dossier. Les portfolios, quant à eux, donnent à voir les projets d’artistes actuellement exposés dans des festivals, des musées ou des galeries.

Novembre est connu pour être le mois de la photographie. À cette occasion, Fisheye #79 en a fait son sujet et répond, au fil de ses pages, à cette vaste question : qu’allons-nous voir ? « Ce numéro a choisi de regarder l’envers du décor. Car l’écosystème de la photographie se construit désormais moins sur des intentions que sur des équations. Écoles, prix, galeries, institutions, foires : chaque étage du circuit a ses comptes à tenir, et ces comptes finissent, sans bruit, par orienter ce qui se produit. Notre dossier “Du premier corpus à Paris Photo” le dit sans fard : l’artiste qui entre dans la machine en ressort “produit fini”, et la moitié des photographes artistes-auteurs déclarent moins de 700 euros de revenus artistiques par an. Pierre Bourdieu publiait Un art moyen en 1965 ; nous voici face à un art des moyens. L’Irlande, elle, a tranché : après trois ans d’expérimentation, elle verse désormais 325 euros par semaine à 2000 artistes tirés au sort. Ailleurs, on continue d’appeler vocation ce qui ressemble furieusement à du bénévolat » , assure Benoît Baume, fondateur du magazine, dans son édito.

Le sens de la photographie

Dans ce numéro, vous retrouverez des événements qui ont lieu pendant le mois de la photographie et s’étendent, pour beaucoup, jusqu’au début de l’année 2027. Outre Paris Photo se comptent a ppr oc he, PhotoSaintGermain ou encore des expositions à la Villa Pérochon, au Jeu de Paume et au musée du Louvre. Nos portfolios s’ouvrent sur un portrait d’agnès b., qui présente 5 jours à Moscou en 1987 , au 17, rue Dieu, à Paris, jusqu’au 13 novembre 2026. Nous retrouvons ensuite Marisol Mendez , exposée au Photaumnales , Maciej Markowicz à la Galerie XII, Victorine Alisse au Festival Mois de la Photo, Jenna Garrett et Frédéric Stucin à 200LUX EXPO , Juliette Pavy à Planches Contact Festival et Summer Wagner à la foire Paris Photo. Notre dossier s’intéresse justement au parcours qui mène à cette dernière. Formations, rencontres, prix photo, livres, galeries, acheteurs, collectionneurs… Si un organigramme le résume de manière schématisée, l’analyse le décrypte en profondeur et évoque des choix qui échappent souvent à l’artiste lui-même. La partie « L’émergence » interroge le sens de la photographie quand la librairie présente deux ouvrages publiés chez Fisheye Éditions : AFP, de l’autre côté des tirages de presse et Didier Lefèvre, les images qui content . Le premier nous plonge dans les coulisses de ces images de travail devenues des œuvres à part entière. Le second rend hommage à un photographe dont le parcours est représentatif de sa génération. La sélection propose, quant à elle, neuf livres qui ont retenu notre attention.

Retrouvez Fisheye #79 dans les kiosques et sur notre boutique en ligne .

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: With more exits expected later this week as Paramount seizes Warner Bros , we hear that the latter’s Head of Communications, Chelsey Summey , has departed the Burbank, CA lot.

Summey first joined Warner Bros as SVP Communications in January 2024 and was later named Head of Communications reporting to Motion Picture bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy . During her tenure she oversaw strategic communications across Warner Bros. Pictures, New Line Cinema, Warner Bros. Pictures Animation, Warner Bros. Clockwork and Warner Bros. Theatre Ventures. In this capacity, she led internal and external communications strategy, advising studio leaders on high-profile business and reputational matters while shaping the narrative around Warner Bros.’ films, talent, and broader business priorities.

Related Stories

Michael De Luca & Pamela Abdy: When They Are Leaving Warner Bros & What’s Next For Them

Skydance Motion Picture Group Co-Chairs Josh Greenstein & Dana Goldberg Say In Day 1 Memo That Film Divisions Will Operate Independently

Summey came to Warner Bros from Amazon MGM Studios, where she served as Head of Corporate Communications for the studio’s film group.

Watch on Deadline

Before that, Summey spent nearly a decade at 20th Century Fox (now 20th Century Studios), where she rose to SVP Corporate Communications overseeing media relations, executive communications, corporate events, talent relations and awards-campaign strategy for the studio as well as the daily operations of the global communications team.

While at Fox, she worked on several award-winning and blockbuster movies including Bohemian Rhapsody , the Deadpool franchise, The Greatest Showman , The Martian , The Revenant , Hidden Figures , Life of Pi and the Ice Age franchise among others. During her tenure, she played an integral role in developing and leading the studio’s crisis communications strategy.

Before Fox, Summey held corporate communications and publicity roles at both Paramount Pictures and CAA.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : Bollywood icons Saif Ali Khan ( Sacred Games ) and Vidya Balan ( Jailer 2 ) will star with Mélanie Laurent ( Inglourious Basterds ) in The Lunchbox filmmaker Ritesh Batra ’s next film Long Years Ago , which is now underway in Mumbai.

The comedy-drama heralds from Adeel Ahmed and writer-director Batra’s film and TV outfit Poetic License, and is being produced in partnership with Jio Studios ( Dhurandhar ), and Good Chaos ( Ballad Of A Small Player ). Jyoti Deshpande is producing for Jio, while Good Chaos’s Mike Goodridge and Teresa Moneo serve as executive producers, as does Siddharth Mehra.

Related Stories

'Unaccustomed Earth': Nisha Ganatra Pulls Out Of Directing; Ritesh Batra Steps In To Helm

Doha Film Festival Unveils 2026 Jury Headed By Naomi Kawase

Set in 1991, Long Years Ago “is the story of a family that has gone too long without saying the things that matter, and what happens when they’re finally forced to find the words.”

Watch on Deadline

“I am tremendously honored to be working with Saif, Vidya and Melanie, and to see these great actors bring characters that are so close to my heart to life,” said Ritesh Batra.

“Ritesh has an extraordinary gift for telling deeply personal stories that resonate across cultures. Long Years Ago is a film about love, family, and the things we often struggle to say to one another, and I felt an immediate connection to it. Collaborating with Melanie, Vidya, and this exceptional team is exciting, and I can’t wait for audiences around the world to experience this deeply moving story,” commented Saif Ali Khan.

“I’m absolutely thrilled to be a part of Ritesh Batra’s next film. I’ve been a huge admirer of his work ever since The Lunchbox , and have been hoping to collaborate with him for the longest time. There’s such a beautiful sensitivity and honesty to his storytelling. What makes this even more special is that I get to reunite with Saif after Parineeta, my very first film! I can’t wait to experience the magic of working with both Ritesh and Saif,” added Vidya Balan.

“I met Ritesh fifteen years ago at the Marrakech Film Festival, and we shared this dream to meet in Mumbai one day. I immediately loved this new project, and I am more than honored and happy to be a part of it,” noted Mélanie Laurent.

Batra made his name with The Lunchbox , which premiered at Cannes and became one of the highest-grossing releases of the year in India. He went on to direct Our Souls at Night with Robert Redford and Jane Fonda, and the Sundance title Photograph , starring Nawazuddin Siddiqui and Sanya Malhotra. Most recently, he directed the first block of the upcoming Netflix series Unaccustomed Earth .

Poetic License also has projects in development with HBO and A24. The company’s theater work began with The Lunchbox Musical , written by Batra and adapted from his 2013 film. The production played a sold-out run at Berkeley Repertory Theatre.

Dil Chahta Hai , Omkara and Sacred Games star Saif Ali Khan, and National Award winner Vidya Balan, are both icons of the screen in their native India. César winner Laurent is known for movies including Inglourious Basterds and Now You See Me .

Former A24 exec Mehra worked on shows including Beef and Mo for Netflix, before launching label Total Monsoon. His first production, Crystal Lake (a prequel series to the Friday the 13th movies from Brad Caleb Kane, Linda Cardellini and A24) premiered on Peacock + Sky on October 15. Upcoming are Superfakes for A24, and Long Years Ago .

article_text:
Editor’s Note: This story was updated on October 23 2026, with additional information.

The Korean Ministry of Culture, Sports, and Tourism will audit You Hong-june, the former director of the National Museum of Korea . You tendered his resignation on Wednesday after a misidentified calligraphic artwork belonging to him was put on display at his museum. The news was announced by multiple South Korean news outlets, including the English language newspaper Korea Herald .

The work in question was presented in the show “The Korean Table: Food, Nature, and Life” (on view through October 25) as a piece by Park Won-geun (1912–50). Park was socialist activist from North Chungcheong who fought against Japanese colonial rule (1910–1945), a dark period in Korean history marked by forced assimilation, loss of individual rights, and exploitation.

A month later, amid outside questions regarding the work’s attribution, the museum removed it from the exhibition; subsequent research confirmed that it was in fact by pro-Japanese bureaucrat Park Jung-yang, who had once used the name Park Won-geun.

You has exhibited and donated other items from his collection to the institution since taking office in 2025, and the incident sparked questions about his influence on the selection of works for exhibitions. While the museum apologized for the mix-up, it did not initially disclose the owner of the piece or how it came to be in the exhibition. You, however, admitted to lending the work, though he denied that the loan was meant to boost the value of an object in his collection. “I did lend the piece from my private collection,” he told JoongAng Ilbo “I also believed the calligraphy was the work of an independence activist. The admission spurred calls for changes to the museum’s verification process.

“A national museum should apply the strictest standards when selecting exhibits, yet it is deeply concerning that works owned or recommended by the director may bypass rigorous curatorial review,” a senior figure in the museum community who requested anonymity told JoongAng Ilbo. “Museum staff must seriously reflect on their responsibility to the public and the museum’s role as a public institution.” On Tuesday, speaking during an annual parliamentary audit of the museum, You Hong-june bowed his head and apologized for the incident. When asked whether he had had the work authenticated before putting it on display, You answered that he had not because he was confident in his attribution, having majored in calligraphy history

“Initially, I did not disclose that the calligraphy . . . was from my personal collection because I thought it might be seen as boasting,” You said. “After it was later identified as a work by Park Jung-yang, I felt ashamed as an art historian. I am ashamed and deeply remorseful.” On Wednesday, You offered to resign his post.

Prior to his appointment as director of Korean National Museum, the world’s third-busiest museum, You was president of the Korean Cultural Heritage Administration between 2004 and 2008. The 77-year-old art historian is best known for writing the popular series of books, “My Exploration of Cultural Heritage,” which were used as textbooks for many Korean university arts courses in the 1990s.
excerpt_original: Director You Hong-june faced scrutiny after loaning the institution a misattributed work from his private collection

article_text:
Believe the hype. “ Wicker ,” now in theaters, is every bit as horny, romantic and wonderful as the trailer leads you to believe.

Olivia Colman plays a spinster fisherwoman in a medieval community where marriage is what gives a woman worth. Although she is a fierce independent woman, the village mocks her as she goes about making her living. One day she goes to the local basket weaver, played by Peter Dinklage, and asks him to make her a wicker husband.

Related Stories

Enter Alexander Skarsgård — yes, that is him under all that makeup — wearing a practical suit and prosthetic makeup to transform him into a basket man.

Popular on Variety

It began with Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson, who were adapting Ursula Wills’ short story “The Wicker Husband.” Weta Workshop artists, prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley and lead makeup FX artist Sarah Rubano received the script and a call from the writers and directors who told them, “We want to make this practically,” says Dunckley. “They wanted a piece of beautiful concept art that showed their vision.”

The pair spent 18 months in research and development alone. Because prosthetic makeup materials are manufactured to imitate human flesh and skin, it posed a challenge. “This guy is made of wicker, so we had to do it a different way,” Dunckley says. He continues, “We tested our theory. We thought that if we could get the strands of the weave to be individual and get them to move as if they were individual muscle fibers that drove his movement, then he could be a believable sentient wicker being.”

But they couldn’t mold it, so the pair were pushed toward modern innovation using 3D digital sculpting and 3D printing.

They began with a full-body scan of Skarsgård so they could sculpt pieces specific to him.

The intricate basket weave was created using a relatively new powder-bed laser-sintered printing process. Dunckley explains, “It’s a volume of thermoplastic elastomer; you shoot a laser into it and where that focal point of the laser is, it fuses the powder and you can build intricate weave and complex geometry. The powder in the bed holds the strands apart while they set.”

And why didn’t Colman get splinters during the film’s steamy bonking scenes?

Nearly all of Skarsgård’s costume was made up of 50 individual 3D-printed appliances that were painted to look like wicker before being stitched onto a suit made out of soft, flexible spandex — so no actual straw was involved.

Dunckley says, “It’s a semiflexible material, not too dissimilar to the feeling of touching proper wicker weave.”

As for the prosthetics, Rubano focused on the makeup, which comprised 10 individual pieces.

Rubano says, “He would get into this very fitted suit and we would bounce between the makeup chair and getting him ready in the suit, depending on the different stages.” She goes on to say, “We had ears, eye bags and lips. We had an underlip piece and a jaw piece, and the larger forehead, nose, cheekbones and there was lots of hand painting around his eyes.”

His facial hair — beard, hair and eyelashes — was constructed from muka, a silky-soft fiber extracted from the harakeke plant. This material allowed them to knot the individual strands onto the weave itself so they could cut and style it like human hair.

The key was not to lose Skarsgård under the makeup. Dunckley says the team used 3D animation software: “We could track the expressive range of the face so that we could engineer into the weave the ability to move for his expression.”

In all, it took under two hours to transform Skarsgård into the wicker husband. “90 minutes is where we were by the end of it,” Rubano says.

Dunckley adds, “The other big piece to the puzzle was Alexander himself. What a wonderful collaborator and team player! He was resilient. He was funny. He was so invested. He would sit as still as a statue in the chair.”

They encountered one small issue. Rubano reveals, “He runs hot; the suit’s kind of hot and it was a hot Hungarian spring.”

And what about the wicker penis?

“There’s been a lot of speculation about just the mechanics of how this would work and about the potential danger of a wicker penis,” Dunckley says. “I think the basket maker, he’s skilled. He’s traveled the world. He’s learned from every culture how to weave, and I think he would know exactly how to weave a wicker ween so it’s user-friendly.”

Rubano credits the film’s costume designers András Dániel Tóth and Attila Godena-Juhász for that detail. “They fabricated the wicker ween for the full-body river shot. They did such a great job because it was very last minute, but it’s puff spandex. The weave was 3D, so there was dimension to it. From a distance, they color-matched it so beautifully.”

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "A Swedish auction house will sell an abstract painting by Hilma af Klint , an artist whose work almost never comes to market.", "links": [{"text": "Hilma af Klint", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/hilma-af-klint/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The painting, titled Ser III No. 5 (1920), will be sold by the Stockholm-based Bukowskis house during a November 19 sale of modern art and design objects. It has been given an estimate of $600,000–$800,000, and if it reaches even its low estimate, the work will shatter af Klint’s prior auction record.", "links": [{"text": "Bukowskis", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/bukowskis/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Once a relatively obscure figure within 20th-century art history, af Klint has come to be seen as a giant of her time . A hit 2018 Guggenheim Museum retrospective in New York credited her with inventing abstraction.", "links": [{"text": "a giant of her time", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/feature/hilma-af-klint-who-is-she-famous-works-1202683824/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Swedish artist’s paintings, often composed of pyramids, looping lines, and flowerlike forms, were inspired by her encounters with spirits from worlds beyond our own. Her spiritualism led her to conceptualize a temple to house her work that was never realized. Her great-grandnephew, who also chairs her foundation, has sought to realize that temple , which would act as a repository for her art and keep it out of museums, but no such plan to open the structure has materialized yet.", "links": [{"text": "sought to realize that temple", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/opinion/hilma-af-klint-art-museums-temple-foundation-controversy-1234735606/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Though af Klint’s work is increasingly being shown in art museums, with the Grand Palais having mounted a survey in Paris earlier this year, it’s unusual to see her work pop up in commercial galleries and on the auction block. So rare are market opportunities that anytime one does happen, it’s considered an event. When David Zwirner gallery exhibited her “Tree of Knowledge” series in 2021, the work was promptly bought by Glenstone , a museum in Potomac, Maryland, founded by Mitchell Rales and Emily Wei Rales.", "links": [{"text": "promptly bought by Glenstone", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/glenstone-museum-hilma-af-klint-acquisition-1234619016/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Af Klint’s foundation has sought to tightly control how her work is shown, which is why it is rarely made available for sale. article_text:
A Swedish auction house will sell an abstract painting by Hilma af Klint , an artist whose work almost never comes to market.

The painting, titled Ser III No. 5 (1920), will be sold by the Stockholm-based Bukowskis house during a November 19 sale of modern art and design objects. It has been given an estimate of $600,000–$800,000, and if it reaches even its low estimate, the work will shatter af Klint’s prior auction record.

Once a relatively obscure figure within 20th-century art history, af Klint has come to be seen as a giant of her time . A hit 2018 Guggenheim Museum retrospective in New York credited her with inventing abstraction.

The Swedish artist’s paintings, often composed of pyramids, looping lines, and flowerlike forms, were inspired by her encounters with spirits from worlds beyond our own. Her spiritualism led her to conceptualize a temple to house her work that was never realized. Her great-grandnephew, who also chairs her foundation, has sought to realize that temple , which would act as a repository for her art and keep it out of museums, but no such plan to open the structure has materialized yet.

Though af Klint’s work is increasingly being shown in art museums, with the Grand Palais having mounted a survey in Paris earlier this year, it’s unusual to see her work pop up in commercial galleries and on the auction block. So rare are market opportunities that anytime one does happen, it’s considered an event. When David Zwirner gallery exhibited her “Tree of Knowledge” series in 2021, the work was promptly bought by Glenstone , a museum in Potomac, Maryland, founded by Mitchell Rales and Emily Wei Rales.

Af Klint’s foundation has sought to tightly control how her work is shown, which is why it is rarely made available for sale. According to the foundation, af Klint herself demanded that her art not be commercialized. A plan to forge a potential relationship between the foundation and David Zwirner fell through after two of af Klint’s descendants inveighed against it. (The family’s controversial stewardship of af Klint’s legacy has reportedly generated disagreement behind the scenes at the foundation.)

Bukowskis said that Ser III No. 5 , one of 85 paintings af Klint produced during a three-month burst of artistic activity in 1920, had been held by the same unidentified collector since 1995. The collector purchased the work after the foundation made “a small number of works” available for sale in the early ’90s, the house stated in its release.

According to Bukowskis, only two of af Klint’s paintings have ever been sold at auction, “both more than 30 years ago.”

It was not clear to what degree, if at all, the Hilma af Klint Foundation was involved in the plan to sell Ser III No. 5 . ARTnews has reached out to the foundation for comment.

article_text:
Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings ended his three-decade association with the company he co-founded last June, but he has a lot to say about how the company can get back to “being thrilling.”

The exec said he “read about” Netflix laying off 1,000 workers , about 6% of its staff, but did not know in advance about this month’s cutbacks.

“It’s hard because I’d like to be in the fray helping,” he said in an appearance on the podcast On with Kara Swisher . “Those are traumatic moments, saying goodbye to some people and getting other people to focus on, ‘OK, we really need to take up our creative excellence and just to be supportive.’ But they’re very competent people. They’ll figure it out. So I’m not worried about it.”

Along with the staff cuts, Netflix also overhauled its executive ranks, replacing content chief Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice and ousting film head Dan Lin . Amid the overhaul, Swisher asked if the company’s new leaders should significantly retool the company’s approach to programming given the recent slowdown in viewership growth.

Watch on Deadline

“I think the strategy is doing more and better television shows, more and better movies,” he replied with characteristic directness.

Hastings added that the company would do well to return to its roots, albeit with newer offerings like live sports now in the mix. “The core brand property is about being thrilling,” he said. “We realized, it took a long time, that we could be distrusted, we could be disliked, but we can never be boring, OK? That the essence of an entertainment brand is to be thrilling.”

The co-founder also weighed in on YouTube, whose share of viewing on TV screens continues to increase as Netflix remains in a holding pattern. He noted key differences between the companies’ business models. “They have 3 million paid creators who are fighting for attention,” he said. While that population occasionally introduces blockbuster cultural properties like Obsession and Backrooms , he said it still represents “an incredibly small amount of viewing on YouTube. And it took a while to develop it. It’s the stuff that’s very attention-grabby. So in hacking attention, YouTube’s platform is very good. … It’s a highly tuned machine for attention and it’s winning viewing hours.”

Asked whether Netflix should lean into short-form fare, Hastings zoomed out to the bigger picture of entertainment’s evolution. “If you look at the beginning of television in the 1950s and 1960s, movie viewing went way down because suddenly there’s this new hot object, television,” he said. “And then movies got a lot better in the 1970s. There was a whole creative revolution in the pacing and the realism. And then movies fought back and became, again, up until the internet or up until Covid, really a substantial art form. So I would say the parallel there is, you know, YouTube is the television and that example and where the movies is we have to take up the creative bar and push ourselves to be ever more gripping, real, connecting, and do what we do – I say we. Which they do incredibly well.”

Swisher pushed Hastings on Netflix’s ill-fated pursuit of an acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery’s studios-and-streaming division, a move that continues to weigh on the company’s stock. The former Netflix chief noted that Paramount paid Netflix a $2.8 billion breakup fee as part of clinching its $110 billion purchase of all of WBD and forming Skydance.

“At the price that we had bid, we were really happy,” Hastings recalled of the jockeying with Paramount. “Then the price went up a bunch and it seemed a bridge too far. … We could have done it. It’s not a ‘can’t,’ but a ‘choose not to.'”

Netflix’s Co-CEO structure, a unique setup in corporate America, was implemented first with Hastings and Ted Sarandos and then with Sarandos and Greg Peters.

Asked why it has worked well at the company, Hastings offhandedly said he didn’t expect it to remain common “over the next 100 years of Netflix.”

Swisher paused on that line, asking Hastings why he believed the company would endure for another century.

“Because I think humans are going to be around, and you love entertainment,” he replied.

title_original: A Protea Is Not a Flower
summary_zh: 开普敦 Zeitz MOCAA 展览《A Protea Is Not a Flower》，展期 2025-10-16 至 2027-06-20。日期来自场馆官网；票价、开放日与预约请核对原文。

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "蔡茨当代艺术博物馆（Zeitz MOCAA）呈献展览《A Protea Is Not a Flower》，由勒拉托·沙迪（Lerato Shadi）和罗宾·罗德（Robin Rhode）共同呈现，呼应格拉德·塞科托（Gerard Sekoto）、贝茜·海德（Bessie Head）以及唐·马特拉（Don Mattera）的生平与创作。展览由蔡茨当代艺术博物馆的卡尼·马维海（Khanyi Mawhayi）策展，展期为2025年10月16日至2027年6月20日。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《A Protea Is Not a Flower》是一场跨代对话，汇聚了南非艺术家与作家，他们的生平与创作都在应对流亡体验的复杂性。当代视觉艺术家勒拉托·沙迪和罗宾·罗德呼应了画家格拉德·塞科托以及作家贝茜·海德和唐·马特拉的生平与作品，这三位是20世纪南非黑人现代主义知识分子运动的重要人物。展览标题灵感来源于马特拉的诗作《Protea...》，该诗通过南非国花的隐喻探讨了殖民主义、种族隔离与爱国主义。如果海神花（Protea）不是一朵花，那它又是什么？自1774年起，原产于南非的海神花种子被传播至世界各地，包括英国、新西兰、澳大利亚和美国加利福尼亚州等地用于商业目的。如同本次展览中的艺术家一样，海神花是一种拥有复杂根系的植物——能够在恶劣条件和多变气候下生存。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览审视了塞科托和海德在海外经历的各种形式的流亡，与马特拉在南非境内忍受的内在孤立之间的相似性。被排斥、在身体、情感和艺术上被剥夺与他人的联系意味着什么？这揭示了罗德和沙迪选择在欧洲生活和执业时所面临的选择质量的什么特质？这些当代艺术家为了在德国柏林建立生活，作出了何种流亡妥协1？展览汲取了塞科托、海德和马特拉的书信文字及其现代主义艺术创作，探索了个人与政治表达的谱系，并切入流亡、身份与记忆的主题。它勾勒出交流的星丛与社群，揭示了这些主角之间深厚的联系，即便在没有任何有记载的相遇的情况下也是如此。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览将塞科托的绘画与沙迪和罗德的装置、摄影和电影并置，在三位艺术家之间构筑了一种概念与形式上的对话。塞科托的《Le Massacre de Sharpeville/Sharpeville Massacre》（1960）与沙迪的《Maropeng》（2022）相遇，将历史与当下的交织呈现在观众面前。罗德的《Twilight》（2012/2013）向马特拉致敬，同时呼应了塞科托《Sketch for Song of the Pick》（n.d.）的节奏与重复。两位当代艺术家均呈现了全新委约的壁画，反思了贯穿整个展览的多重流亡形式。", "translated": true}, "https://zeitzmocaa.museum/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Lerato-Shadi-300x201-jpg.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Zeitz MOCAA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "勒拉托·沙迪是一位南非艺术家，目前在德国柏林生活和工作。沙迪于2006年毕业于约翰内斯堡大学，获视觉艺术文学士学位，并于2018年获得柏林白湖艺术学院空间策略文学硕士学位。沙迪的创作横跨行为、录像和装置，她质疑既定的殖民叙事，并批判将历史抹去作为针对边缘化人群暴力的机制的做法。她挑战黑人女性气质的表征政治，通过在重复的干预中使用自己的身体来聚焦其生活经验。她运用时间和持续性来反思劳工及其在社会中的价值，其行动和手势充当了诉说平庸事物的仪式化特质的装置。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "沙迪自2007年起举办了多场个展，近期展出包括：南非开普敦Blank Projects的《Tsela e e motsopodia》（2025）；德国柏林柏林图姆画廊的《Maropeng》（2022）。她还参与了众多国际和本土群展，其中包括：荷兰鹿特丹布鲁图斯的《Everything Is True—Nothing Is Permitted》（2025）；南非开普敦诺瓦尔基金会的《We, The People: 30 Years of Democracy in South Africa》（2024）；德国波恩联邦艺术大厅的《Who We Are: Reflecting a Country of Immigration》（2023）等。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "罗宾·罗德（Robin Rhode）", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://zeitzmocaa.museum/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Robin-Rhode-300x199-jpg.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Zeitz MOCAA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "罗宾·罗德是一位多学科艺术家，目前在德国柏林生活和工作。罗德介入城市的建筑环境，将人们的注意力吸引到某一地点及其周边往往不为人知的历史和社会状况上。罗德的艺术实践从青年街头文化和艺术史中汲取等量的灵感，将城市墙壁视作无限延伸的画布。他运用了一系列视觉策略和媒介——包括绘画、行为艺术和摄影——来创作出令人惊叹且具有批判性的艺术作品，拒绝停滞不前并保持运动状态，抗拒任何单一的定义。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "罗宾·罗德自2003年起举办了多次个展，近期的展览包括：德国柏林诺克画廊的《Fragments in the Sun》（2025年）；美国纽约利盟画廊的《African Dream Root》（2023年）；荷兰瓦森纳沃林登博物馆的《Robin Rhode》（2022年）。罗德近期的群展包括：法国巴黎交易所商业中心的《Corps et âmes》（2025年）；美国洛杉矶郡艺术博物馆的《Imagining Black Diasporas: 21 st -Century Art and Poetics》（2025年）；挪威奥斯陆基斯特弗斯博物馆的《Ring of Fire》（2025年）；英国伦敦维多利亚与阿尔伯特博物馆的《Fragile Beauty: Photographs from the Sir Elton John and David Furnish Collection》（2024年）等。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关于作家贝西·海德", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://zeitzmocaa.museum/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Bessie-Head-300x201-jpg.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Zeitz MOCAA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝西·海德（1937–1986年生），是一位南非小说家，其一生充满孤立与流亡。海德出生于南非彼得马里茨堡一家精神病院的白人母亲，曾在两个寄养家庭生活，后在青春期再次被送入国家照管机构。她被送往德班的圣莫妮卡之家（一个英国圣公会传教孤儿院），并在那里完成了高中教育。她被拒绝发放护照，被迫于1964年持单程出境签证离开南非前往博茨瓦纳。她曾短暂做过教师，随后在一家政府所有的农场做体力劳动者，之后成为全职作家。1968年，她出版了自己的第一部小说《When Rainclouds Gather》——她用小说的收益在塞罗韦建造了自己亲切地命名为“雨云（Rainclouds）”的家并开辟了一座花园。1979年，海德获得博茨瓦纳国籍，并于1986年逝世，生前再未回到她的出生地南非。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝西·海德最为人熟知的小说是《When Rainclouds Gather》（1968年）、《Maru》（1971年）和《A Question of Power》（1973年）。她的作品过去是、现在也依然是她作为一名流亡的混血女性，在饱受殖民与种族暴力摧残的地区生活经验的写照，同时也诉说着许多试图在动荡与困境中谋生并维系生活的南部非洲黑人群体的经历。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关于作家唐·马特拉", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://zeitzmocaa.museum/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Don-Mattera-300x202-jpg.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Zeitz MOCAA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "唐·马特拉（1935–2022年生）是南非作家、诗人、记者兼活动家。他出生于索菲亚敦，在德班的一所修道院学校度过了成长岁月，随后返回索菲亚敦与祖母同住。年轻时，马特拉加入了当地最臭名昭著的帮派之一。正是在这段时期，他作为一名诗人和活动家找到了自己的声音，后来作为政治活动家加入了非洲国民大会青年联盟。他作为诗人和记者的写作对种族隔离政府进行了尖锐的批评，导致他在1973年至1982年间屡遭禁令并多次被软禁。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "马特拉出版了多部著作，包括《They Passed This Way and Touched our Lives》（2008年）、《Inside the Heart of Love》（1997年）、《Memory is the Weapon》（1987年）和《Azanian Love Song》（1983年）。1986年，他荣获瑞典笔会颁发的库尔特·图霍夫斯基奖。他曾担任《星期日泰晤士报》（The Sunday Times）、《每周邮报》（The Weekly Mail）和《索韦托人报》（The Sowetan）的记者，并于1990年担任《邮报与卫报》（The Mail and Guardian）艺术与文化版块的编辑。马特拉曾获得多项大奖和荣誉，包括纳塔尔大学以及威特沃特斯兰德大学授予的文学荣誉博士学位。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "关于画家热拉尔·塞科托", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://zeitzmocaa.museum/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Gerard-Sekoto-198x300-jpg.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Zeitz MOCAA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "热拉尔·塞科托（1913–1993年生）是南非艺术家兼音乐家，被广泛视为南非黑人现代主义绘画的先驱之一。塞科托出生于德兰士瓦郊外的一个小型德国路德会传教站，他选择了艺术生涯，并于1938年搬到索菲亚敦。1940年，塞科托成为第一位有作品被南非博物馆（约翰内斯堡美术馆）收藏的黑人艺术家。1947年，塞科托带着自我流亡的心态离开南非前往巴黎，试图在这个他眼中的世界艺术中心确立自己的地位。1993年，他在法国巴黎逝世。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在他生命的晚年，塞科托的作品获得了国际认可，部分归功于芭芭拉·林多普（Barbara Lindop）出版的一本专著。他被法国政府授予艺术与文学骑士勋章，并被南非政府追授伊卡曼加勋章（Order of Ikhamanga），以表彰他对艺术的贡献。1989年，塞科托还被威特沃特斯兰德大学授予荣誉博士学位。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "近期展出热拉尔·塞科托作品的展览包括：美国圣路易斯米尔德里德兰恩肯珀艺术博物馆的《African Modernism in Africa》（2023年）；南非开普敦A4艺术基金会的《Common》（2023年）；南非开普敦蔡茨当代艺术博物馆的《When We See Us》（2022年）；南非比勒陀利亚比勒陀利亚大学雅韦特艺术中心的《Handle with Care》（2022年）等。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "图片鸣谢：勒拉托·沙迪。摄影：Select Image。由蔡茨当代艺术博物馆提供。罗宾·罗德。摄影：蒂尔曼·福格勒（Tilman Vogler）。由艺术家提供。贝西·海德。照片由外部提供。唐·马特拉。照片由外部提供。热拉尔·塞科托。摄影：乔治·哈利特（George Hallett）。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Zeitz MOCAA presents A Protea Is Not a Flower , an exhibition with Lerato Shadi and Robin Rhode responding to the life and works of Gerard Sekoto, Bessie Head and Don Mattera. Curated by Zeitz MOCAA’s Khanyi Mawhayi, the exhibition opens on 16 October 2025 and runs until 20 June 2027."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A Protea Is Not a Flower is a multigenerational conversation between South African artists and writers whose lives and works contend with the complexity of the exilic experience. Contemporary visual artists Lerato Shadi and Robin Rhode respond to the lives and works of painter Gerard Sekoto and writers Bessie Head and Don Mattera, three important figures of the Black Modernist Intellectual Movement in twentieth-century South Africa. The exhibition’s title is inspired by Mattera’s poem Protea…, which addresses colonialism, apartheid, and patriotism through the metaphor of South Africa’s national flower. If a protea is not a flower, then what is it? From 1774, the Protea’s seeds—indigenous to South Africa—were spread to geographies across the world, including England, New Zealand, Australia, and California, USA for commercial purposes. Like the artists in this exhibition, the protea is a plant with a complex root system—able to survive under harsh conditions and varying climates."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The exhibition considers the parallels between the various forms of exile experienced by Sekoto and Head abroad, and the internal isolation that Mattera endured within South Africa. What does it mean to be excluded, stripped of your connection to others physically, emotionally, and artistically? What does it reveal about the quality of choices available to Rhode and Shadi in choosing to live and practice in Europe? What kinds of exilic compromises 1 did these contemporary artists make to build lives for themselves in Berlin, Germany? Drawing on the written correspondences of Sekoto, Head, and Mattera, as well as their modernist artistic output, the exhibition explores the spectrum of personal and political expression, navigating themes of exile, identity, and memory. It maps constellations and communities of exchange, revealing the profound connections between these protagonists, even in the absence of any documented encounters."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Including paintings by Sekoto alongside installations, photography, and film by Shadi and Rhode, the exhibition proposes a conceptual and formal dialogue between the three artists. Sekoto’s Le Massacre de Sharpeville/Sharpeville Massacre (1960) meets Shadi’s Maropeng (2022), confronting the viewer with the entanglement of history and the present. Rhode’s Twilight (2012/2013) pays homage to Mattera while responding to the rhythm and repetition of Sekoto’s Sketch for Song of the Pick (n.d.). Both contemporary artists present newly commissioned murals that reflect on the multiple forms of exile threaded through the exhibition."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The artists all push up against, paint on, and carve into walls. This is made literal in Rhode and Shadi’s practices as they transform these structures of containment and concealment into ephemeral works that speak to migration, inclusion, home, and exile. The exhibition stages an intergenerational conversation wherein the foreign communes with the familiar, asking: what happens when we allow ourselves to look Beyond the Gate (1946-47), beyond borders, and beyond the national identities inherited from coloniality?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Zeitz MOCAA’s exhibition and curatorial programming is generously supported by the Mellon Foundation and BMW South Africa."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "meet the artists"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Lerato Shadi"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://zeitzmocaa.museum/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Lerato-Shadi-300x201-jpg.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Zeitz MOCAA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Lerato Shadi is a South African artist currently living and working in Berlin, Germany. Shadi graduated from the University of Johannesburg in 2006 with a Bachelor of Arts in Visual Art and completed her Master of Arts in Spatial Strategies from the Weißensee Academy of Art in Berlin in 2018. Working across performance, video, and installation, Shadi interrogates assumed colonial narratives and critiques practices of historical erasure as mechanisms of violence against marginalised peoples. She challenges the politics of representing Black womanhood, centring her lived experience by using her body in repetitive interventions. She employs time and duration to reflect on labour and its value in society, with her actions and gestures functioning as devices that speak to the ritualistic quality of the mundane."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Shadi has held multiple solo shows dating since 2007 with recent presentations including, Tsela e e motsopodia, Blank Projects, Cape Town, South Africa (2025); Maropeng, Galerie im Turm, Berlin, Germany (2022). She has also participated in numerous group exhibitions both internationally and locally, including Everything Is True—Nothing Is Permitted , Brutus, Rotterdam, Netherlands (2025); We, The People: 30 Years of Democracy in South Africa , Norval Foundation, Cape Town, South Africa (2024); Who We Are: Reflecting a Country of Immigration, Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn, Germany (2023), among others."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Robin Rhode"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://zeitzmocaa.museum/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/Robin-Rhode-300x199-jpg.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Zeitz MOCAA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Robin Rhode is a multi-disciplinary artist currently living and working in Berlin, Germany. article_text:
Zeitz MOCAA presents A Protea Is Not a Flower , an exhibition with Lerato Shadi and Robin Rhode responding to the life and works of Gerard Sekoto, Bessie Head and Don Mattera. Curated by Zeitz MOCAA’s Khanyi Mawhayi, the exhibition opens on 16 October 2025 and runs until 20 June 2027.

A Protea Is Not a Flower is a multigenerational conversation between South African artists and writers whose lives and works contend with the complexity of the exilic experience. Contemporary visual artists Lerato Shadi and Robin Rhode respond to the lives and works of painter Gerard Sekoto and writers Bessie Head and Don Mattera, three important figures of the Black Modernist Intellectual Movement in twentieth-century South Africa. The exhibition’s title is inspired by Mattera’s poem Protea…, which addresses colonialism, apartheid, and patriotism through the metaphor of South Africa’s national flower. If a protea is not a flower, then what is it? From 1774, the Protea’s seeds—indigenous to South Africa—were spread to geographies across the world, including England, New Zealand, Australia, and California, USA for commercial purposes. Like the artists in this exhibition, the protea is a plant with a complex root system—able to survive under harsh conditions and varying climates.

The exhibition considers the parallels between the various forms of exile experienced by Sekoto and Head abroad, and the internal isolation that Mattera endured within South Africa. What does it mean to be excluded, stripped of your connection to others physically, emotionally, and artistically? What does it reveal about the quality of choices available to Rhode and Shadi in choosing to live and practice in Europe? What kinds of exilic compromises 1 did these contemporary artists make to build lives for themselves in Berlin, Germany? Drawing on the written correspondences of Sekoto, Head, and Mattera, as well as their modernist artistic output, the exhibition explores the spectrum of personal and political expression, navigating themes of exile, identity, and memory. It maps constellations and communities of exchange, revealing the profound connections between these protagonists, even in the absence of any documented encounters.

Including paintings by Sekoto alongside installations, photography, and film by Shadi and Rhode, the exhibition proposes a conceptual and formal dialogue between the three artists. Sekoto’s Le Massacre de Sharpeville/Sharpeville Massacre (1960) meets Shadi’s Maropeng (2022), confronting the viewer with the entanglement of history and the present. Rhode’s Twilight (2012/2013) pays homage to Mattera while responding to the rhythm and repetition of Sekoto’s Sketch for Song of the Pick (n.d.). Both contemporary artists present newly commissioned murals that reflect on the multiple forms of exile threaded through the exhibition.

The artists all push up against, paint on, and carve into walls. This is made literal in Rhode and Shadi’s practices as they transform these structures of containment and concealment into ephemeral works that speak to migration, inclusion, home, and exile. The exhibition stages an intergenerational conversation wherein the foreign communes with the familiar, asking: what happens when we allow ourselves to look Beyond the Gate (1946-47), beyond borders, and beyond the national identities inherited from coloniality?

Zeitz MOCAA’s exhibition and curatorial programming is generously supported by the Mellon Foundation and BMW South Africa.

meet the artists

Lerato Shadi

Lerato Shadi is a South African artist currently living and working in Berlin, Germany. Shadi graduated from the University of Johannesburg in 2006 with a Bachelor of Arts in Visual Art and completed her Master of Arts in Spatial Strategies from the Weißensee Academy of Art in Berlin in 2018. Working across performance, video, and installation, Shadi interrogates assumed colonial narratives and critiques practices of historical erasure as mechanisms of violence against marginalised peoples. She challenges the politics of representing Black womanhood, centring her lived experience by using her body in repetitive interventions. She employs time and duration to reflect on labour and its value in society, with her actions and gestures functioning as devices that speak to the ritualistic quality of the mundane.

Shadi has held multiple solo shows dating since 2007 with recent presentations including, Tsela e e motsopodia, Blank Projects, Cape Town, South Africa (2025); Maropeng, Galerie im Turm, Berlin, Germany (2022). She has also participated in numerous group exhibitions both internationally and locally, including Everything Is True—Nothing Is Permitted , Brutus, Rotterdam, Netherlands (2025); We, The People: 30 Years of Democracy in South Africa , Norval Foundation, Cape Town, South Africa (2024); Who We Are: Reflecting a Country of Immigration, Bundeskunsthalle, Bonn, Germany (2023), among others.

Robin Rhode

Robin Rhode is a multi-disciplinary artist currently living and working in Berlin, Germany. Rhode intervenes in the built environment of the city, drawing attention to the often-unseen histories and social conditions of a site and its surroundings. Taking inspiration equally from youth street culture and art history, Rhode’s artistic practice treats the city wall as an expanded canvas. He employs a range of visual strategies and media— including painting, performance, and photography—to create surprising and critical artworks that refuse stasis and remain in motion, defying any singular definition.

Rhode has held numerous solo exhibitions since 2003, with recent presentations including, Fragments in the Sun, Noack Gallery, Berlin, Germany (2025); African Dream Root , Lehmann Maupin, New York, United States (2023); Robin Rhode , Museum Voorlinden, Wassenaar, Netherlands (2022). Rhode’s recent group shows include Corps et âmes , Bourse de Commerce, Paris, France (2025); Imagining Black Diasporas: 21 st -Century Art and Poetics , Los Angeles County Museum of Art, United States (2025) ; Ring of Fire , Kistefos Museum, Oslo, Norway (2025); Fragile Beauty: Photographs from the Sir Elton John and David Furnish Collection , Victoria and Alfred Museum, London, United Kingdom (2024), among others.

About Bessie Head, Writer

Bessie Head (b. 1937–1986), was a South African novelist whose life was marred by periods of isolation and exile. Born to a white mother in a mental hospital in Pietermaritzburg, South Africa, Head lived with two foster families before being remanded into state care again during her adolescence. She was sent to Santa Monica’s Home, an Anglican mission orphanage in Durban, where she completed her high school education. She was denied a passport, forcing her to leave South Africa on a one-way exit visa to Botswana in 1964. She worked briefly as a teacher, and then as a labourer on a government owned farm, before becoming a full-time writer. She published her first novel When Rainclouds Gather in 1968—the proceeds of which she used to build her home, affectionately named ‘Rainclouds’ and establish a garden in Serowe. In 1979, Head was granted citizenship in Botswana, passing away in 1986, having never returned to her birth country of South Africa.

Bessie Head is best known for her novels When Rainclouds Gather (1968), Maru (1971) and A Question of Power (1973). Her body of work was, and continues to be, a reflection not only of her experience as an exiled mixed-race woman in a region disfigured by colonial and racial violence but also speaks to the experiences of many Black Southern Africans attempting to make and sustain life amid tumult and difficulty.

About Don Mattera, Writer

Don Mattera (b. 1935–2022) was a South African writer, poet, journalist and activist. Born in Sophiatown, he spent his formative years at a convent school in Durban before returning to Sophiatown to live with his grandmother. In his youth, Mattera became involved with one of the most notorious gangs and was eventually. It was during this time that he found his voice as a poet and activist, later joining the African National Congress Youth League as a political activist. His writing, both as a poet and journalist, was sharply critical of the apartheid government, resulting in banning orders and a series of house arrests between 1973 and 1982.

Mattera published several books, including They Passed This Way and Touched our Lives (2008), Inside the Heart of Love (1997), Memory is the Weapon (1987), and Azanian Love Song (1983). In 1986, he received the Kurt Tucholsky Award from the Swedish PEN Club. He worked as a journalist for The Sunday Times, The Weekly Mail , and The Sowetan and in 1990 served as editor of The Mail and Guardian Arts and Culture section . Mattera received numerous awards and accolades, including an Honorary Doctorate in Literature from the University of Natal as well as the University of the Witwatersrand.

About Gerard Sekoto, Painter

Gerard Sekoto (b. 1913–1993) was a South African artist and musician, widely regarded as one of the pioneers of Black South African modernist painting. Born at a small German Lutheran mission station just outside Transvaal, Sekoto chose a career in the arts, and moved to Sophiatown in 1938. In 1940, Sekoto became the first Black artist to have an artwork acquired by a South African museum, the Johannesburg Art Gallery. In 1947, Sekoto left South Africa for Paris under self-imposed exile, seeking to establish himself in what he saw as the centre of the art world. He passed away in 1993 in Paris, France.

Towards the end of his life, Sekoto gained international recognition for his work, in part due to a monograph published by Barbara Lindop. He was designated a Chevalier des Arts et des Lettres by the French government and posthumously awarded the Order of Ikhamanga for his contribution to the arts by the South African government. In 1989, Sekoto was also granted an honorary doctorate from the University of the Witwatersrand.

Recent exhibitions of Gerard Sekoto’s work include African Modernism in Africa, Mildred Lane Kemper Art Museum, St. Louis, USA (2023); Common, A4 Arts Foundation, Cape Town, South Africa (2023); When We See Us , Zeitz MOCAA, Cape Town, South Africa, (2022); Handle with Care, Javett Art Centre, University of Pretoria, Pretoria, South Africa (2022), among others.

“ Capturing Bigfoot ” doesn’t waste time getting to the hairy meat of the matter. It opens with the shaky, grainy 16mm footage that’s the most widely viewed piece of cinéma vérité in history apart from the Zapruder film. It even looks like the Zapruder film — though the setting, in this case, is a woods, full of birch trees and sunlight and vivid autumn color. For a few moments, the image jerks around in a raw amateur way. Then it grows steadier, and there, about 100 feet away from the camera, an ape-like figure walks along in front of the forest foliage, turning its head for an instant to look at the cameraman, then continuing on its way.

This famous evidence of the creature known as Bigfoot was shot by a man named Roger Patterson in Northern California on Oct. 20, 1967. The footage lasts just 59 seconds. We don’t get to spend much time gawking at the creature (it’s only a tantalizing glimpse), but he’s there just long enough for us to notice several things. The hair on his back looks a bit shiny . And is it our imagination, or is this primitive creature not just walking but strolling , with a rather jaunty sense of purpose?

Why did this footage possess the world? As an opening title informs us, “No one has ever been able to determine whether the film is real or a hoax.” Then it adds, “Until now.” “Capturing Bigfoot” is an astounding documentary about the legend of Bigfoot — about how it was born, how it took hold, and how that iconic piece of film footage came to be. It’s a documentary that answers all the questions and solves all the mysteries. Unlike your typical film about UFOs, it doesn’t leave you with that vague feeling of “The truth is still out there, and I’m still not sure what it is.” “Capturing Bigfoot” shows you the truth, but what it really shows you is what that truth says about us, a society that went down the rabbit hole of wanting to believe and now, increasingly, lives there.

“Capturing Bigfoot” is being released at the perfect moment, when belief in the uncanny has been given a new “credibility” by the testimony of select U.S. military officials about the reality of UAPs — but, at the same time, certain legendary mythologies about an existence beyond ours have now been unmasked as hoaxes. For decades, the 1934 photograph of the Loch Ness Monster was a haunting image of a lost world. In 1994, it was revealed that two men had created that image out of wood putty attached to a toy submarine. And in 1991, Doug Bower and Dave Chorley explained that they created the crop-circle phenomenon by going into a field and making one, in 1978, after an evening spent at a pub. As someone who’d spent many hours gawking in wonder at photographs of crop circles, I greeted the revelation of that hoax with a crestfallen fascination. I no longer flirted with the teasing possibility that crop circles could have been created by a force from another world. Somehow, though, the melting down of that possibility made our own world seem smaller.

But the Bigfoot legend never loomed in that way, at least not for me, because there was always something fishy about it. Starting with this: If there was a “Bigfoot” living in the woods of Northern California in the late 1960s, wouldn’t it have been seen by someone other than Roger Patterson and his camera? Marq Evans, the director of “Capturing Bigfoot,” digs into the Bigfoot legend with an investigator’s wide-eyed curiosity and cunning. For a while, he zeroes in on Patterson, the Zapruder of the saga, who died in 1972. The film goes back to paint a portrait of this eccentric resident of Yakima, Wash., who became obsessed with the idea of oversize simian humanoids going back to the late ’50s.

Patterson, with his light drawl and camera-ready affability, might have stepped out of the ancient version of an Errol Morris film, back when Morris was the snarkster of “Gates of Heaven.” His obsession was touched off by an article in True magazine in 1959 (we see the article; it was entitled “America’s Abominable Snowman”). And, of course, the legend that Bigfoot emerged from had actually been around for centuries, going back to the Himalayan myth of the Yeti (in British Columbia, it became the Sasquatch).

Patterson would take his young son on camping trips in a VW van into the mountains of Northern California, on the lookout for Bigfoot. He would stuff two live horses into the van — an indication, right there, that he had a bit of a screw loose. But he was cosplaying at being a cowboy. He was a rodeo rider, and with his rifle and cowboy hat and drawling aw-shucks attitude, he made himself into a camera-ready character. His ingenuity was in tapping into what we might, at the time, have called National Enquirer culture: its tall tales and its legion of readers. This was the true silent majority of the new America. We see old footage of interviews with people who claim to have had Bigfoot sightings, which are just like the interviews with people who claim to have had alien encounters.

Patterson’s son, Clint, now in his late 60s, is the documentary’s central figure. He resembles Bill Paxton, and he’s like a Bill Paxton character . “When I came out of my mom’s vagina,” says Clint, “they put a cowboy hat on me.” He means that literally. (It tells you what you need to know about this family.) Clint, for most of “Capturing Bigfoot,” remains a true believer in his dad’s 59-second Bigfoot film. And there are expert witnesses who testify as to why it has to be authentic. One is Dr. Jeff Meldrum, a professor of anatomy at Idaho State University, where he’s got an “Evolutionary Morphology Laboratory” that’s essentially a Bigfoot room, with models, evidence, and an example of the 16mm camera Roger Patterson used. Meldrum says that watching the footage, he can identify detailed muscle groups in Bigfoot, and that the creature is clearly real. (One interesting detail: The Bigfoot we see in the footage is female . She has mammary glands.) And Bill Munns, who worked as a make-up artist at Universal Studios starting in 1969, explains that the image of Bigfoot in the footage could not have been a man in a costume. Even Hollywood, he says, did not have the technology at the time to make an ape-man look that good.

But then the movie starts to piece together the story of how the footage came into existence. Roger Patterson was, among other things, a canny DIY visual artist who, in 1966, wrote and published a book about Bigfoot entitled “Do Abominable Snowmen of America Really Exist?” It was illustrated with his lavish drawings. And Clint Patterson talks about how as a boy, he once went into his father’s shed, which was usually locked, and found a pile of second-hand fur coats.

Using his 59-second film, Roger Patterson was able to turn Bigfoot into a phenomenon. He went on the talk-show circuit (Johnny Carson, Merv Griffin, Art Linkletter), making himself into a found-object celebrity. The Bigfoot footage, as Clint puts it, “went viral before the word viral even existed.” It was given credibility by being featured in scientific magazines, as if it were an anthropological discovery . And the film, in its Zapruder-like “authenticity,” was seen, in its very semiotics, as a document of something real. Patterson played it in movie theaters, on a road-show tour, charging $2 a ticket, then moving on to the next town. In the Salt Palace in Salt Lake City, one of his associates recalls that “We played two weeks after Simon and Garfunkel, and took more money out of the building than they did.”

The money, which added up to many millions in today’s dollars, was a blessing and a curse. Much of it went, mysteriously, to Patterson’s brother-in-law, Al DeAtly, who used it to rescue his construction company, fashioning himself into the lead contractor in the state of Washington (where he built a country mansion as large and gaudy as Mar-a-Lago). But one of Patterson’s closest and most loyal associates, Bob Gimlin (interviewed in the documentary), got nothing. That said, he is still on the Bigfoot convention circuit.

On the dark underside of the 59-second Bigfoot film lies a tawdry family drama. There is greed and infighting, all buried in the murk of a secret that must be maintained at all costs. Marq Evans uncovers the secret. He has assembled his movie with resounding suspense, and he finds the smoking gun. It is a lost 16mm film shot in 1966, the year before the famous Bigfoot footage, and what it shows is a kind of rehearsal for it. We also meet an associate of Patterson’s, a man named Bob Hieronymus, who has a very familiar loping walk.

“Capturing Bigfoot” reveals that the 1967 footage of Bigfoot was a hoax, and in that sense you could say that the story is over and done with. Roger Patterson was a classic American snake-oil salesman who figured out how to con the media age. But one of the key themes of the documentary is that Patterson, with his ingenious little fake film, didn’t just create an outlandish legend. He created a reality that took on a life of its own. He created the “evidence” to make magical thinking real, and I don’t think it’s overstating things to say that you can draw a direct line from the true-believer world of Bigfoot to the true-believer world that so many exist in today, whether it’s UAP obsession or the wacked conspiracy theory that says the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Bigfoot or no Bigfoot, we’re all living on the Planet of the Ape Believers.

‘Capturing Bigfoot’ Review: An Astounding Documentary Uncovers the Truth

Reviewed online, Oct. 12, 2026. Running time: 103 MIN.

Production: An XYZ Films release of an XYZ Films, The McCaw production, in association with Creative House. Producers: Tamir Ardon, Marq Evans, Nick Spicer. Executive producers: Douglas Hamm, Lara Hamm, Kate Bolotin, Aram Tertzakian.

Crew: Director: Marq Evans. Camera: Jason Roark. Editor: Michelle M. Witten. Music: Jonathan Sadoff.

With: Clint Patterson, Bob Gimlin, Bob Heironimus, Greg Long, Jeffrey Meldrum, Bill Muns, Teresa Brooks, Larry Lund.

article_text:
After 12 years, three standalone movies and a holiday special, Amanda Seyfried appears to have no regrets turning down a Guardians of the Galaxy lead role.

The Oscar nominee explained that the MCU role of Gamora was “just not for me,” noting she made the decision “for my family” to not take on the character, which was ultimately played by Zoe Saldaña .

“I think turning down Guardians of the Galaxy was just so obvious to me at the time,” she explained in a Q&A with SAG-AFTRA Foundation. “I’m like, ‘This is not going to be a hit. The tree and the raccoon are talking to each other. And also they’re all in space.’ And I was just like, ‘This will ruin my career if this is bad. And there’s a high chance that this could be bad.'”

Related Stories

Amanda Seyfried Joins Ramy Youssef’s ‘Martha & Muhammad’ At A24

James Gunn Hints More ‘Guardians of the Galaxy’ Stars Will Join DCU

Seyfried continued, “I mean, obviously I was wrong. But I still don’t take back that decision. I made it for myself. I made it for my family that I knew I wanted to have. And I just don’t want to spend all the time in the makeup trailer. I just can’t sit still anyway. I really don’t like stunts, and I don’t like heights, and I don’t like pretending the entire world. I need something to hold on to.”

Watch on Deadline

Starring opposite Chris Pratt’s Star-Lord, Saldaña starred as the green-skinned alien assassin in Guardians of the Galaxy (2014), Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (2017) and Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 3 (2023), as well as 2022’s The Guardian of the Galaxy Holiday Special . She also played the character in Avengers: Infinity War (2018) and Avengers: Endgame (2019).

article_text:
写真家・三浦憲治の個展「三浦憲治写真展 2026 ミウラヒロシマ Vol.13」が、2026年9月8日から14日まで、東京・恵比寿のALで開催される。2014年から故郷・広島をテーマに毎年発表を続けてきた「ミウラヒロシマ」シリーズの第13回となる。

1949年広島市生まれの三浦は、東京写真短期大学在学中に写真家・長濱治に師事。雑誌『MCシスター』でキャリアをスタートさせる一方、ピンク・フロイドやレッド・ツェッペリンなど、来日した海外ミュージシャンのライブを撮影するようになる。その後も松任谷由実、矢沢永吉、YMO、井上陽水、奥田民生など、日本の音楽シーンを代表するアーティストたちを数十年にわたって撮影。ステージ上の決定的な瞬間からアーティストの素顔まで、音楽と並走するように数多くの写真を残してきた。

そんな三浦が2014年から継続しているもうひとつの重要な仕事が、自身の出身地を見つめる「ミウラヒロシマ」だ。長年にわたりミュージシャンや音楽の現場にカメラを向けてきた写真家が、毎年故郷へと立ち返り、その時々の広島を撮影し、発表を重ねてきた。

13回目を迎える今回も、一度きりの撮影によって土地を記録するのではなく、同じ場所へ繰り返し足を運び、時間の蓄積とともに変化する広島を見つめるシリーズの現在地を紹介する。

タイトル

三浦憲治写真展 2026 ミウラヒロシマ Vol.13

場所

AL（東京都渋谷区恵比寿南3-7-17）

会期

2026年9月8日（火）〜14日（月）

時間

13:00〜19:00（最終日18:00）

休み

無休

料金

無し

URL

https://al-tokyo.jp/gallery/miurahiroshima2026/

article_text:
Tree Week: Sarah Hood Salomon: Under the Overpass

©Sarah Hood Salomon, Copycat, from Under the Overpass

We tend to notice trees when they are beautiful, enormous, or planted exactly where we expect them to be. The trees that grow in the cracks of a city, under freeways, beside construction sites, or in whatever scraps of dirt they can find are easier to overlook. But perhaps those are the trees worth paying attention to. They have adapted to a landscape that was never designed with them in mind, quietly making a place for themselves alongside the rest of us.

Sarah Hood Salomon ‘s Under the Overpass looks closely at these overlooked trees and the strange, often uneasy relationship between nature and the cities we build. There is something almost human about their persistence—bent, constrained, surrounded by concrete, yet continuing to grow. The photographs invite us to slow down and consider these trees not simply as part of the urban landscape, but as witnesses to it. They have been there through construction, neglect, change, and expansion, quietly recording a neighborhood’s history while adapting to whatever comes next. There is beauty in that resilience, but also a reminder that survival is not the same thing as being cared for.

An interview with the artist follows and for the next 3 days, Salomon will contribute features to Tree Week.

©Sarah Hood Salomon, Shadows and Silhouettes, from Under the Overpass

Sarah Hood Salomon is a fine art photographer, whose work is based on quiet observation of trees within urban environments. Her images tell stories of their survival, Trees are sometimes viewed as a nuisance, but many cities are taking steps to ensure their protection. The relationship is a complicated one.

Sarah’s award-winning images have been included in numerous solo and group shows throughout the U.S. Sarah is also a photography judge, curator, author and lecturer. She received her MFA in photography from Maine Media College. Her work is represented by Multiple Exposures Gallery in Alexandria, VA.

Instagram: @sarahhoodsalomon

©Sarah Hood Salomon, Two Dead Trees, from Under the Overpass

Under the Overpass

My work is rooted in a deep admiration for the remarkable adaptability of trees. Our human judgment categorizes certain trees as beautiful, while others are perceived as ugly, dangerous, or invasive. This project, Under the Overpass, examines the complex relationships between humans and the natural environment and the many ways in which trees acclimate to human encroachment in urban areas.

It is my belief that every tree holds a story. Whether struggling to survive in a small patch of exhausted dirt or encased in scaffolding shielding it from construction, trees are a living history of their neighborhoods and a microcosm of our changing world. They are an essential part of cleansing urban air, and reducing the rising temperatures of global warming. The presence of trees softens the harsh lines of a cityscape and reduces anxiety and depression, making our cities a safer place to live.

My aim is to raise awareness of the condition of urban trees and promote the care and preservation of this valuable resource. The challenge is to combine development with sustainability. Despite the encroachment of urban areas, trees survive and evolve at a pace of life that is hard to comprehend. Their endurance and patience with us is commendable.

title_original: Pedigree chums: why the movies are killing off fewer dogs
editorial_title_zh: 纯种同伴：为什么电影里死狗的镜头越来越少了
editorial_excerpt_zh: 电影人是否担心因为弄死一只狗狗而疏远日益敏感的观众？还是说，人类现在已经太娇气，无法承受《古惑丑拍档》带来的创伤？曾几何时，就在不久以前，看电影还是一件分明的事情。会有好人，也会有……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "曾几何时，就在不久以前，看电影还是一件分明的事情。会有好人，也会有坏人，而你之所以能认出谁是坏人，是因为他们会朝一只狗的脸上开枪。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种事情发生的频率比你想象的还要高。《疯狂的麦克斯2》，狗中枪了。《复仇》，狗中枪了。《古惑丑拍档》，狗中枪了。《赤焰战场》，狗中枪了。《持枪的人》，狗中枪了。《荒漠怪客》，狗中枪了。《突击队员》，你绝对猜不到。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "但事情变化得真快。如今——要么是因为政治正确走火入魔，要么是因为基本的人类 decency（体面），或者诸如此类的原因——电影里狗狗被谋杀的可能性要小得多了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "宠物保险公司 Lassie 的一项研究（当然是这家公司）发现，在2020年至2025年间，电影中狗狗死亡的数量惊人地下降了80%。报告指出，6年前，在票房收入最高的前100部电影中，有10部出现了狗狗在银幕内或银幕外死亡的情节。但到了2025年，这一数字降至仅有2部。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现在，这可能归结于无数原因中的任何一个。第一个、也可能是最重要的原因是，电影业正处于岌岌可危的境地。整个媒介的未来命悬一线，每一美元都至关重要，所以为什么要冒着因为无缘无故弄死一只小狗而疏远一大批观众的风险呢？情况是如此糟糕，以至于出现了一个专门的网站——“那只狗死了吗？”（Does the Dog Die?）——纯粹是为了警告观众任何会破坏观影乐趣的犬只死亡情节。", "links": [{"text": "Does the Dog Die?", "url": "https://www.doesthedogdie.com/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ed6af2bcbe67dc7b2d38e144f30f1ba78f1b2018/0_0_1190_1553/master/1190.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "汤姆·汉克斯坐在沙发扶手上，身旁是一只名叫胡奇的大型棕色狗狗", "caption": "没有剧透……汤姆·汉克斯与胡奇。照片：Cinetext Collection/Sportsphoto/Allstar", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，我们对银幕上与动物相关的死亡变得如此敏感，以至于它被视为《Digger》票房惨败的一个潜在原因。毕竟，该片的预告片着重展示了 Digger 那只患病被宣判绝症的猫。现在，显而易见那是一只故意做得粗糙的电子动画道具猫，但这并没有阻止“那只狗死了吗？”的大量用户警告人们它的死讯。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为观众，我们是如此紧张，以至于电影制作人在拍摄狗狗电影时，甚至不能不明确向我们保证这些动物能安然无恙地活下来。早在6月，布拉德·皮特的新狗狗电影《Heart of the Beast》的制片人理查德·雷蒙德（Richard Raymond）就在社交媒体上直接剧透了自己电影的结局，只为了让我们安心，他在推特上写道：“狗没死。不客气。”", "links": [{"text": "“The dog does not die. You’re welcome.”", "url": "https://x.com/curbyourchichi/status/2065096267299275213"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "然后是安妮·海瑟薇，她的电影《The End of Oak Street》讲述了一个家庭、一只狗和一只极度饥饿的霸王龙的故事。在这部（12A级）电影的宣传期间，海瑟薇含蓄地向观众保证这只狗不会变成恐龙的点心，她宣称：“我觉得杀死狗狗的电影应该自动被评为R级。”", "links": [{"text": "“I feel like movies that kill dogs should automatically be rated R.”", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/p/Db9FEOQDT5H/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当然，然而，这让我怀疑安妮·海瑟薇其实并没有看过她所有的电影。她今年票房最高的是克里斯托弗·诺兰的《奥德赛》（The Odyssey），其中包含了一个绝对无缘无故的狗狗死亡镜头，简直可以说是到了滑稽的程度。简而言之，一只狗被扔下了悬崖。它对故事核心重要吗？不，它跟故事甚至连边都沾不上。它只是发生了。太阳升起。太阳落下。约翰·雷吉扎莫把一只小狗从悬崖边扔了下去。", "links": [{"text": "The Odyssey", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/the-odyssey"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "显然海瑟薇在这里说错了。如果对狗狗死亡自动给予R级评级，将会改变我们所知的电影质感。在《古惑丑拍档》中，胡奇的死是整部电影的关键所在。它是否给整整一代以为自己买票看搞笑狗狗电影的儿童留下了永久的心理创伤？是的。但它是否也起到了让我们更好地面对残酷世界现实的作用？同样是的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0efe2fb5a11c451cdc60d0bec2af3f1ac0a9bd20/0_0_2650_1766/master/2650.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "安妮·海瑟薇和两个受惊的女孩带着一只狗站在下雨的公交车站", "caption": "当情况变得艰难时……安妮·海瑟薇与狗狗伙伴在《The End of Oak Street》中。照片：Ent-movie/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "也许这正是我们大家所需要的。我们生活在一个极度不确定的时代，有时感觉我们仍然没有为等待着我们的恐怖做好充分准备。所以问问自己：现在是把我们自己小心翼翼地保护起来、远离那些让我们心烦意乱的事物的时候，还是电影制作人应该重新开始承担责任、尽可能多地弄死一些狗的时候？不管这是什么类型的电影，无论是剧情片、恐怖片还是《汪汪队立大功》动画片。让我们强加一个强制性的犬只死亡配额来让我们重新坚强起来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "谁跟我一起？没有人？那如果只是《汪汪队立大功》呢？如果只是《汪汪队立大功》里的阿奇呢？还是没有？随你们便吧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "电影", "links": [{"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/film"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "动物", "links": [{"text": "Animals", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/animals"}], "translated": article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "T here was a time, not so long ago, when watching a film was a clearcut experience. There would be a good guy and a bad guy, and you would know who the bad guy was because they would shoot a dog in the face."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It happened more times than you might expect. Mad Max 2, dog gets shot. Revenge, dog gets shot. Turner & Hooch, dog gets shot. Red, dog gets shot. Man with the Gun, dog gets shot. Badlands, dog gets shot. Dog Soldiers, you’ll never guess."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But how things change. These days – thanks to either political correctness gone mad or basic human decency or whatever – dogs are much less likely to be murdered in films."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A study by (of course) pet insurance firm Lassie has discovered that the number of dogs that die in movies dropped by a whopping 80% between 2020 and 2025. It reports that six years ago, 10 of the 100 highest-grossing films featured a dog dying either on or off screen. But by 2025, this number fell to just two."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Now, this could be down to any number of reasons. The first, and possibly most important, is that cinema finds itself in a perilous position. The future of the entire medium is at stake and every dollar counts, so why risk alienating a swathe of the audience by gratuitously offing a pup? Things are so bad that there is an entire website – Does the Dog Die? – purely to warn viewers of any enjoyment-spoiling canine fatalities.", "links": [{"text": "Does the Dog Die?", "url": "https://www.doesthedogdie.com/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/ed6af2bcbe67dc7b2d38e144f30f1ba78f1b2018/0_0_1190_1553/master/1190.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Tom Hanks sits beside Hooch, a large brown dog, perched on a sofa armrest", "caption": "No spoilers … Tom Hanks and Hooch. Photograph: Cinetext Collection/Sportsphoto/Allstar", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In fact, we may have become so sensitive to animal-related deaths onscreen that it has been offered as one potential reason for the Digger flop. After all, the film’s trailer heavily focused on Digger’s sick cat as it was given a terminal diagnosis. Now obviously it was a deliberately bad animatronic prop cat, but that didn’t stop large numbers of Does the Dog Die?’s users from warning people of its death."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So nervous are we as an audience that film-makers cannot even make dog movies without explicitly reassuring us that the animals are going to make it out OK. As early as June, Richard Raymond – the producer of Brad Pitt’s new canine movie Heart of the Beast – took to social media to literally spoil the ending of his own film, just to set our minds at rest, tweeting: “The dog does not die. You’re welcome.”", "links": [{"text": "“The dog does not die. You’re welcome.”", "url": "https://x.com/curbyourchichi/status/2065096267299275213"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And then there’s Anne Hathaway, whose film The End of Oak Street concerns a family, a dog, and a very hungry T rex. During promotion for the (12A) film, Hathaway tacitly managed to reassure audiences that the dog wasn’t going to become dino chow, by stating that “I feel like movies that kill dogs should automatically be rated R.”", "links": [{"text": "“I feel like movies that kill dogs should automatically be rated R.”", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/p/Db9FEOQDT5H/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Of course, however, this leads me to suspect that Anne Hathaway hasn’t actually watched all of her films. Her highest-grossing of the year was Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey , which features a dog death so absolutely gratuitous that it legitimately borders on slapstick. In short, a dog gets hurled off a cliff. Is it central to the story? No, it isn’t even remotely peripheral to the story. It’s just a thing that happens. The sun rises. The sun sets. John Leguizamo lobs a puppy off the side of a cliff.", "links": [{"text": "The Odyssey", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/the-odyssey"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Obviously Hathaway is wrong here. An automatic R-rating for a dog death would change the texture of films as we know them. In Turner & Hooch, Hooch’s death was the entire point of the movie. Did it permanently traumatise a generation of children who thought they had signed up for a funny dog flick? Yes. But did it also work to brace us better against the cruel realities of the world? Also yes."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0efe2fb5a11c451cdc60d0bec2af3f1ac0a9bd20/0_0_2650_1766/master/2650.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "Anne Hathaway and two startled girls with a dog stand at a rainy transit stop", "caption": "When the going gets ruff … Anne Hathaway and canine companion in The End of Oak Street. Photograph: Ent-movie/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "And perhaps that’s what we all need. We live in deeply uncertain times, and sometimes it feels like we still aren’t fully prepared for the horrors that await us. So ask yourself this: is this the right time to cosset ourselves away from things that upset us, or is it time that film-makers started to act responsibly again by killing as many dogs as they possibly can?
